Title: Physical connectivity between Pulley Ridge and Dry Tortugas coral reefs under the influence of the Loop Current/Florida Current system
Brief Abstract: The Pulley Ridge and Dry Tortugas coral reefs are among the most pristine, but also fragile, marine ecosystems of the continental United States. Understanding connectivity processes between them and with surrounding shelf and deep areas is fundamental for their management. This study focuses on the physical processes related to the connectivity of these reefs. Unprecedented in situ time series were used at these specific reef locations, together with satellite observations and numerical simulations, to investigate the dynamics controlling local circulation on the Southwestern Florida Shelf (SWFS) under oceanic influence. The approach of the Loop Current and Florida Current (LC/FC) system to the SWFS slope can induce 0.5 to 1m/s offshore flows impacting the Pulley Ridge and Dry Tortugas reefs. On the other hand, when the LC/FC system retreats from the slope, onshore flows can carry open-sea waters over the coral reefs. Local formation of cyclonic eddies is possible near the Dry Tortugas reefs in the LC approach case and passage of upstream LC Frontal Eddies is possible in the LC retreat case. Offshore currents 1m/s over the SWFS slope were also found during periods of anticyclonic LC Eddy separation. A novel finding is the shedding and northward propagation of mesoscale anticyclonic eddies from the core of the LC along the West Florida Shelf. Eddy shedding may have a broader effect on the dynamics of the shelf around the study reef areas. Long periods of LC/FC domination over these coral reefs (reaching several weeks to months) are characterized by strong (1m/s) along-shelf currents and continuous upwelling processes, which may weaken the slope stratification and bring colder, deeper waters over the shelf-break and toward the shallower shelf region.

Title: Research activities in Earth System Modelling. Report No. 55. WCRP Report No. 08/2025
Brief Abstract: This is an annual (or periodic) compilation of short research articles and summaries on global activities in Numerical Experimentation and Climate/Earth System Modelling. It serves as a non-peer-reviewed collection/report documenting ongoing research, developments, and advancements in Earth system models (ESMs), numerical weather prediction (NWP), climate modeling, and related fields from institutions worldwide. The report highlights emerging technologies, model improvements, and collaborative efforts in the community. It is compiled by the WCRP-ESMO International Project Office (ESMO IPO) in collaboration with the Working Group on Numerical Experimentation (WGNE) panel members and WCRP support. Explicitly noted as not an official WMO or WCRP publication and not peer-reviewed.

Title: Atmospheric River Analysis and Forecast System (AR-AFS)
Brief Abstract: This repository hosts the workflow and supporting infrastructure to build, install, configure, and run the Atmospheric River Analysis and Forecast System (AR-AFS), a high-resolution regional modeling system developed for analyzing and forecasting atmospheric rivers (ARs) - narrow corridors of intense water vapor transport that drive extreme precipitation, flooding, and water supply issues, particularly along the U.S. West Coast.AR-AFS is built on the Unified Forecast System (UFS) framework using the FV3 dynamical core (Finite-Volume Cubed-Sphere), with ~3 km horizontal resolution over the Northeast Pacific and Western North America domains. It ingests initial and boundary conditions from the operational GFSv16 (Global Forecast System) to produce up to 5-day forecasts. The system emphasizes accurate precipitation guidance for AR landfall events, including fine-scale structures in watersheds and orographic enhancement. Physics suites include Thompson microphysics, EDMF-TKE PBL, GFDL surface layer, Noah land surface, RRTMG radiation, and Scale-Aware Mass-Flux (SAMF) convection (with options to disable convection for tests).The repo provides end-to-end operational-style support: source code compilation, fixed data linking, Rocoto workflow orchestration (for job scheduling on NOAA HPCs), parameter configs, job scripts, and utilities. It supports real-time or retrospective runs on systems like Gaea/C6, Hera, Orion/Hercules, with sample GFS input paths. It's designed for NOAA-internal evaluation, sensitivity testing (e.g., domain stretching via Extended Schmidt Gnomonic grid, convection impacts), and advancing AR forecast skill toward higher NOAA readiness levels.

Title: Updates to NOAA's Unified Forecast System's Cumulus Convection Parameterization Scheme between GFSv16 and GFSv17
Brief Abstract: This study outlines the updates made to cumulus convection parameterizations between Global Forecast System, version 16 (GFSv16), and the forthcoming GFSv17 which will be the first global forecast application to become operational under the Unified Forecast System infrastructure. The updates, addressing known systematic errors and biases, incorporate innovations such as stochasticity, three-dimensional subgrid organizational effects, and a prognostic closure evolution. The changes are shown to improve tropical temperature/humidity biases, convective available potential energy (CAPE) forecasts, CONUS precipitation, and tropical variability. By examining individual updates' impact on temperature, humidity profiles, and precipitation power spectra, we find that the new prognostic closure and stricter precipitation evaporation criteria alleviate a dry and cold bias in the tropical boundary layer and enhance precipitation variability in the tropics. Stricter triggering criteria also allow for more CAPE buildup, particularly over the tropics. The cumulus convection updates have a modest impact on precipitation skill scores over CONUS, but overall, there is an improvement when comparing GFSv16 and the latest GFSv17 prototype configurations, in particularly for larger thresholds. The study also highlights the challenges in developing convection parameterizations suitable for both coupled and uncoupled model configurations. Evaluation of the MJO shows varying responses to cumulus convection changes depending on whether the model is coupled with a dynamic ocean model.

Title: HRRRCast: a data-driven emulator for regional weather forecasting at convection allowing scales
Brief Abstract: The High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model is a convection-allowing model used in operational weather forecasting across the contiguous United States (CONUS). To provide a computationally efficient alternative, we introduce HRRRCast, a data-driven emulator built with advanced machine learning techniques. HRRRCast includes two architectures: a ResNet-based model (ResHRRR) and a Graph Neural Network-based model (GraphHRRR). ResHRRR uses convolutional neural networks enhanced with squeeze-and-excitation blocks and Feature-wise Linear Modulation, and supports probabilistic forecasting via the Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM). To better handle longer lead times, we train a single model to predict multiple lead times (1h, 3h, and 6h), then use a greedy rollout strategy during inference. When evaluated on composite reflectivity over the full CONUS domain using ensembles of 3 to 10 members, ResHRRR outperforms HRRR forecast at light rainfall threshold (20 dBZ) and achieves competitive performance at moderate thresholds (30 dBZ). Our work advances the StormCast model of Pathak et al. by: a) training on the full CONUS domain, b) using multiple lead times to improve long-range skill, c) training on analysis data instead of the +1h post-analysis data inadvertently used in StormCast, and d) incorporating future GFS states as inputs, enabling downscaling that improves long-lead accuracy. Grid-, neighborhood-, and object-based metrics confirm better storm placement, lower frequency bias, and higher success ratios than HRRR. HRRRCast ensemble forecasts also maintain sharper spatial detail, with power spectra more closely matching HRRR analysis. While GraphHRRR underperforms in its current form, it lays groundwork for future graph-based forecasting. HRRRCast represents a step toward efficient, data-driven regional weather prediction with competitive accuracy and ensemble capability.

Title: HRRRCast (Live Pipeline) / NOAA-GSL/HRRRCast-live
Brief Abstract: This repository contains the end-to-end operational/live pipeline for running HRRRCast, NOAA's experimental neural network-based, data-driven emulator for high-resolution regional weather forecasting at convection-allowing scales (3 km grid over CONUS). It serves as the production-ready implementation of the system described in the associated arXiv preprint (2507.05658 / "HRRRCast: a data-driven emulator for regional weather forecasting at convection allowing scales").The pipeline ingests HRRR initial conditions (analyses/forecasts) and GFS boundary conditions, performs preprocessing (per-variable/level normalization, enhanced APCP/precipitation handling, HRRRmodel downsampling, GFSHRRR interpolation), runs either deterministic or probabilistic/diffusion models (e.g., ResHRRR or similar architectures from the paper), generates forecasts (e.g., out to multiple hours/leads), exports outputs in NetCDF and GRIB2 formats (for compatibility with operational systems), and includes plotting/diagnostic tools. It supports ensemble generation (multiple members), unified logging, resilient data downloading, and HPC/SLURM job submission. Key enhancements include probabilistic forecasting via diffusion models (DDIM-style), better handling of longer leads via multi-lead training and greedy rollout, and improved storm placement/detail compared to traditional HRRR in some metrics. This is the "live" version used for real-time experimental forecasts, integrated into NOAA efforts like Project EAGLE (Experimental AI Global and Limited-area Ensemble).

Title: hourly_nest branch in the repository guoqing-noaa/global-workflow
Brief Abstract: This branch (hourly_nest) is an experimental/development fork/branch of NOAA's global-workflow repository, focused on implementing or testing hourly nesting capabilities within the global numerical weather prediction (NWP) workflow.The parent repository provides the end-to-end "superstructure" workflow for running NOAA's operational and developmental global models, including the Global Forecast System (GFS), Global Ensemble Forecasting System (GEFS), and Seasonal Forecast System (SFS), all based on the Unified Forecast System (UFS) weather model (which uses the FV3 dynamical core). It handles tasks like data assimilation (via GSI and JEDI/GDASApp), model integration, post-processing, and runs on NOAA HPC systems (e.g., WCOSS2, Hera, Orion) or cloud environments (e.g., AWS via EPIC/ParallelWorks).The hourly_nest branch specifically targets enhancements for hourly cycling (more frequent data assimilation/forecast cycles, e.g., every hour instead of 6-hourly) combined with nesting features (likely one-way or two-way nested high-resolution grids within the global domain, similar to moving nests in HAFS or regional applications like RRFS). This could enable higher temporal resolution for rapid-update forecasting, better handling of convection or severe weather, or experimental upgrades toward future GFS versions (e.g., GFSv17+ development on the develop branch). It aligns with broader NOAA/EMC/UFS efforts for improved resolution, sub-hourly to medium-range predictions, and innovations in data assimilation/physics/infrastructure under projects like UFS-R2O (Research-to-Operations).Documentation for the main repo is at https://global-workflow.readthedocs.io/, covering cloning, building, linking components, and running experiments - the branch likely modifies workflow scripts, job submission configs, or nesting logic (e.g., in ush/, jobs/, parm/, or model input namelists) to support hourly nested configurations.

Title: Thompson-Eidhammer Microphysics Parameterization for Operations (TEMPO)
Brief Abstract: This repository contains the source code for TEMPO, a modular microphysics parameterization scheme designed to predict clouds and precipitation processes in Earth-system numerical models. It is an operational-grade continuation and evolution of the widely used Thompson microphysics scheme (originally developed for the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model and run operationally in NOAA's High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) system). TEMPO includes enhancements such as aerosol-aware processes, two-moment graupel with predicted density (hail-aware capabilities), improved representation of mixed-phase and winter precipitation, and better compatibility with modern frameworks. It is built as a standalone submodule for easy integration into various host models, with a focus on operational numerical weather prediction (NWP), climate modeling, and high-resolution forecasting. Key goals include maintainability, independent development, and support for convection-allowing scales (e.g., in RRFSv2 development). It supports aerosol-cloud-precipitation interactions and is being adapted for the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) in UFS-community contexts.
